entities.summary:
Agathodaemon of Alexandria, a Greek or Hellenized Egyptian cartographer, is primarily known for his presumed role in the visual representation of Claudius Ptolemy's monumental geographical work, the *Geographia*, likely active during the 2nd century AD within the intellectual hub of Roman Alexandria. While his exact dates and biographical details remain elusive, scholarly consensus posits him as the individual responsible for translating Ptolemy's extensive mathematical coordinates into the earliest known world maps, thereby providing a crucial visual dimension to the textual descriptions of the known world. His work, or the tradition he represents, stands as a testament to the sophisticated Hellenistic scientific tradition that flourished under Roman rule.

The core achievement attributed to Agathodaemon is the creation of the twenty-six maps — one world map and twenty-five regional maps — that accompany most surviving manuscripts of Ptolemy's *Geographia*. These maps, meticulously constructed from Ptolemy's latitude and longitude data, offered an unprecedentedly detailed and mathematically grounded depiction of the oikoumene, stretching from the Fortunate Isles in the west to Serica (China) in the east, and from Thule in the north to the sources of the Nile in the south. This synthesis of mathematical theory and practical cartography was revolutionary, providing a systematic framework for understanding global geography that would dominate Western thought for over a millennium.
